Mandarin Chinese.text: The English word "mandarin" originally meant an official of the Ming and Qing empires.
Mandarin Chinese.evidence: The English word "mandarin" (from Portuguese mandarim, from Malay menteri, from Sanskrit mantrī, mantrin, meaning 'minister or counsellor') originally meant an official of the Ming and Qing empires.

Hindi.text: The name was borrowed from Persian Hindī, meaning "of or belonging to Hind (India)".
Hindi.evidence: It was borrowed from Classical Persian هندی Hindī (Iranian Persian pronunciation: Hendi), meaning 'of or belonging to Hind (India)' (hence, 'Indian').

Modern Standard Arabic.text: Used in literature, media and law, but generally not spoken as a first language, much like Latin today.
Modern Standard Arabic.evidence: MSA is the language used in literature, academia, print, mass media, and law and legislation, though it is generally not spoken as a first language, similar to Contemporary Latin.

Urdu.text: In the late 18th century it was known as Zaban-e-Urdu-e-Mualla, "language of the exalted camp".
Urdu.evidence: In late 18th century, it was known as Zaban-e-Urdu-e-Mualla زبانِ اُرْدُوئے مُعَلّٰی means language of the exalted camp.
